Just when we thought we were out, they pulled us back in. As the entire filmmaking industry shifts after the landmark merger between Paramount and Warner Bros., two of Hollywood's most iconic legacy studios, the trends that moviegoers embraced over the last year now face their greatest threat yet. 2025/2026 signaled a new era for the industry, headlined by two original movies, Sinners and Obsession, that became box office behemoths and cultural sensations. These films and other surprise hits, along with the disappointment of franchise films that were once considered financial guarantees, were supposed to be the catalysts for a new wave of movie-making that showed interest in fresh ideas, rather than sequels, IP, and old brands. The Paramount-WB merger, now operating as Skydance, is the culmination of this unfortunate industry trend. Despite Skydance CEO David Ellison's claim that he is a "believer" in original storytelling, the company's upcoming movie lineup suggests that they are doubling down on safe, familiar franchises. Within no time, Deadline reported that the new mega studio had enlisted Stephen Spielberg and Michael Bay to revive the Transformers franchise.

The combined forces of Paramount and Warner Bros. result in a vast pool of IP ripe for further big-screen adaptations. Just to name a few, Skydance now has ownership of the aforementioned Transformers, DC Comics characters, Harry Potter, Star Trek, the Middle-earth saga, Barbie/Mattel, and many more. Each franchise has a new movie or series in the works, many of which were inherited from Warner Bros., such as The Batman: Part II, the Potter HBO series, and a rumored sequel to Greta Gerwig's 2023 mega blockbuster. It's hard to imagine that Paramount was pursuing a $110 billion acquisition of WB without wanting to capitalize on its lucrative properties, even if the company's newly developed indie/arthouse label, Clockwork, remains intact. Ellison and company have promised to give their major releases a proper theatrical release, but if the majority of their output is going to be franchise-oriented, then the business will be back to square one.

blocks.x: Warner Bros.' final years as an autonomous studio will likely be remembered fondly by cinephiles — an era overseen by Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy, who will not be part of Ellison's management team. At a time when the arts frequently capitulate to shareholders, De Luca and Abdy were among the last bastions of upholding creative freedom and backing auteur filmmakers in the major studio system. Under their leadership, Warner Bros. released a handful of original films that were both beloved and commercially successful, notably Sinners and Weapons, as well as the Best Picture-winning One Battle After Another. Of course, considering that they invested in polarizing movies with unconventional sensibilities, they also greenlit a fair share of noisy flops, including Mickey 17, The Bride!, and Digger, the latter of which released concurrently with the official approval of the merger.

A business merger of this magnitude doesn't go through to take financially reckless decisions, such as lending $100–200 million to Bong Joon-ho, Maggie Gyllenhaal, and Alejandro G. Iñárritu to make provocative black comedies with elaborate concepts and sets. And with all this IP under their belt, Skydance doesn't have to look too far to churn out a profit. While it appears that audiences will have to suffer from a continued onslaught of safe, predictable franchise entries and reboots, keep in mind that legacy brands and superheroes on their own no longer guarantee a blockbuster. Recent flops/financial disappointments like Supergirl, Scream 7, Masters of the Universe, and Star Wars: Mandalorian and Grogu suggest that audience tastes have moved on.

Box office numbers prove that most audiences want something familiar, but it has to present itself as fresh, as evidenced by the rise of new films with pre-established fanbases from other media like Minecraft and Backrooms. The media landscape is not too inspiring from afar, but if the market still dictates how decisions are made, then we can expect more breakthroughs like Sinners and Obsession.
